title: Why does the dollar dominate the world?
subtitle: Bretton Woods, 1944
subject: comprendreLeMonde
description: In 2022, short of dollars, Sri Lanka could no longer pay for its fuel and high-school students stayed home. How did the currency of a single country become the money of the whole planet?
author: mark-n-hoffman

hero.hook: When a country runs out of dollars, its school vans stop: the currency of one nation has become the money of the entire world.

blocks.text: In **April 2022**, Jithmini's school van had no fuel. At **17**, the young Sri Lankan could no longer get to school. Her country's central bank was saving its scarce dollars for essential imports, starting with fuel. Tax cuts and the collapse of tourism had set off a currency crisis.

Outside the United States, many businesses invoice in dollars, banks lend in dollars, and governments keep [[foreign exchange reserves]] in dollars to pay abroad and cope with emergencies. A Sri Lankan importer who owes dollars to a supplier has to find them before the cargo can leave. Why do so many sellers accept only dollars? It is a long story.

sections.title: 1944: America has the gold, the goods and the money

blocks.text: World War II gave the United States unprecedented weight over the world's monetary rules. Its factories produced surpluses at a time when Europe's factories, roads and ports lay in ruins. During and after the war, it held **most of the gold** used for international payments, and it was the planet's great creditor.

blocks.caption: A 12.5-kilo gold bar, the standard format of central bank reserves, on display at a Swiss money museum.

blocks.text: Europe needed food, fuel and machinery. American companies could sell them, but wanted dollars, which European countries, their industries devastated, struggled to earn through exports. Loans and aid would later fill part of the gap. When **44 delegations** met in New Hampshire in **1944**, they were writing the rules for a world in which America had the goods, the gold and the money to lend.

sections.title: Bretton Woods: the dollar, gold and Keynes

blocks.text: At the [[Bretton Woods Conference]], delegates agreed to hold their currencies at a fixed value against the dollar, adjustable in case of serious trouble. The United States promised to exchange the dollars held by foreign governments for gold, at **35 dollars an ounce**. Other currencies were pegged to the dollar, and the dollar to gold.

blocks.caption: A conference room at the Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, where the July 1944 conference was held (recent photo).

blocks.text: [[John Maynard Keynes]], negotiating for Britain, wanted to go further: countries would settle their mutual debts in a new unit, the [[bancor]], and those selling far more than they bought would be pushed to correct course, just like those buying too much. The American team, backed by its gold, preferred a fund that lent national currencies. The agreement created the [[International Monetary Fund]]; the bancor and most of the pressure on surplus countries stayed on paper.

sections.title: 1971: the end of the golden age

blocks.text: By the late 1960s, foreigners held more dollars than American gold could cover at the fixed price. Some governments asked to convert their dollars into gold. In **August 1971**, President Nixon stopped honoring the promise. By **1973**, the major currencies had moved to [[floating exchange rates]]: their value now varied with the market.

blocks.caption: Richard Nixon on television in 1952, nearly twenty years before his August 1971 decision on the dollar.

blocks.text: Yet the bills still arrived in dollars, and banks still wanted to be repaid in dollars. Governments kept dollars in their reserves, often as [[U.S. Treasury bonds]], loans to the American government that are easy to buy and sell. Each use of the dollar made the next one more predictable, safer and simpler. No gold promise was needed to collect an old loan: the contract called for dollars, and so did the new contracts.

In March 2020, the Federal Reserve opened temporary lines to supply dollars to nine more foreign central banks. Half a century after the end of the gold promise, demand for dollars still surges in a crisis.

Central banks still hold dollars, about **57%** of the reported foreign exchange reserves in early 2026 according to the IMF, and businesses still invoice and borrow in dollars. If the dollar gradually lost its lead, new contracts could be written in euros or another currency, central banks would shift their holdings, and the American government, less courted by foreign lenders, would pay more to borrow. Old dollar loans, though, would still be payable in dollars.

events.title: Bretton Woods
events.detail: 44 delegations peg their currencies to the dollar, and the dollar to gold.

events.title: End of the gold promise
events.detail: Nixon stops converting foreign governments' dollars into gold.

events.title: Floating exchange rates
events.detail: The major currencies float against the dollar.

events.title: Dollar lines
events.detail: The Federal Reserve supplies dollars to nine more central banks.

events.title: Crisis in Sri Lanka
events.detail: Short of dollars, fuel runs out and school vans stop.

blocks.text: Changing the currency written on Sri Lanka's fuel invoice would not have filled the tank of Jithmini's van. The country would still have needed money the seller accepts, drawn from its exports, its reserves or a loan. The name of the currency may change, but the problem remains: gathering enough of it to pay for what one imports.

The dollar dominates because the America of 1944 had the gold, the goods and the money, and then because every dollar invoice and every dollar loan made the next one more natural: the gold promise vanished in 1971, the habit stayed.
